title: This Is the Best-Performing Magnificent Seven Stock of 2026. Is It Still a Buy?
detail:
This Is the Best-Performing Magnificent Seven Stock of 2026. Is It Still a Buy?
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool

NVDA
AAPL
^GSPC
META
TSLA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The "Magnificent Seven" is a grouping of stocks used to describe some of the largest companies in the world that have helped lead the U.S. stock market higher over the past decade. It is made up of:

Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL)

Nvidia

Microsoft

Alphabet

Amazon

Meta Platforms

Tesla

For U.S.-listed stocks, all seven of these are in the top 10, so being on this list is a big deal. However, 2026 hasn't been the greatest year for the Magnificent Seven. The S&P 500 is up about 12.3% this year, and only three stocks are outperforming it: Apple, Amazon, and Microsoft. But which one of these is doing the best? It's the non-AI one.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Apple leads all Magnificent Seven stocks

The top performer so far in 2026 has been Apple, up about 29%. That's practically double the second-best performer, Amazon, which has risen around 15%. So, what has separated Apple from the competition? I think there are two reasons.

First, Apple really isn't an AI stock. While its products have some AI features, it's not spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data centers like every other company on this list (besides Nvidia, which is selling the equipment for these data centers). As a whole, the market has been a bit bearish on the AI buildout lately, and Apple has been a haven for investors who aren't as keen on the long-term prospects of AI.

In fact, Apple is the only stock among the top 10 largest companies on U.S. exchanges that doesn't have significant AI investments or business cases riding on the AI buildout. This has made it a safe haven for non-AI investors and has boosted its stock.

Another reason Apple has done well this year is that its iPhone 17 lineup was the most popular of any of its previous models. This has driven sales growth and has made Apple a respectable business again.

However, Apple's day of reckoning could be coming. Outside of Tesla (which has a sky-high valuation of 424 times trailing earnings), Apple is by far the most expensive stock in the Magnificent Seven.

NVDA PE Ratio data by YCharts

As a result, I think the stock could be getting a bit too pricey, and investors need to watch out. Apple's strong performance this year hasn't come entirely from business results, and if the market flips its stance on AI and becomes bullish on it again, Apple's stock could sell off in favor of some AI-focused investments. It's about as good as it gets for Apple sentiment right now. As a result, I don't think Apple stock is a buy right now.

We just published a list of the 10 Best Dow Stocks to Buy for 2027 and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) ranked 7th on this list.

Yahoo Finance reported on November 5 that the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled 3.4%, or more than 1,800 points, while the S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5% into correction territory. Chip stocks took the brunt of the damage, with AI chip designers and memory makers among the hardest hit. The slide erased the gains from a day earlier, when the Dow had jumped 3% for its best session of 2026 after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, Yahoo Finance wrote on November 4. By mid-session Thursday, the index was heading for its worst second day after a midterm election in data going back to 1896, the outlet noted.

Amazon (AMZN): AWS Grew 39%, and Management Expects Growth Above 40% in 2027 and 2028
The Dow's Safe-Haven Run Cracks

For most of the week, the Dow had looked like the sheltered corner of the market. Yahoo Finance reported on November 2 that the Dow edged up 0.4% while the Nasdaq dropped roughly 1% as investors rotated out of technology names and into consumer cyclical and financial services shares, which left the Dow looking like the market's relative winner. On Thursday, that cushion gave way, as the focus turned to what a Democratic Congress could mean for the AI buildout, and for the data centers driving it in particular. You might also be interested in reading our piece on how the AI chip leader's growth compares with the cloud software giant's.

The reversal was fast and violent. Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at an equity research firm, pointed out that the VIX volatility index posted its biggest one-day jump in more than two years. It took the Nasdaq just six minutes on Thursday to erase its entire post-election rally, and even Wednesday's winners such as the iPhone maker turned lower. That Wednesday buying had been helped by falling oil prices, while the Windows maker jumped 6% to a record high.

A Jobs Report Steadies the Tape

Friday brought a partial rebound. Yahoo Finance reported on November 6 that the US added 165,000 jobs in October, and the Nasdaq gained 1.9% while the S&P 500 rose 1% and the Dow added 0.1%. For a closer look at one of the biggest AI spenders caught in the sell-off, we recently covered why the search giant's low price-to-earnings ratio can mislead. The stronger jobs data lifted Treasury yields and kept Federal Reserve policy at the center of market attention, Reuters reported on November 6, as the price-weighted index of 30 major US companies held roughly flat.

title: Europe Wants €6 Billion From Cheap Parcels. Temu’s Owner PDD Trades at 7x Earnings

Europe Wants €6 Billion From Cheap Parcels. Temu’s Owner PDD Trades at 7x Earnings
Rexielyn Diaz

AMZN
Trade AMZN on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Europe Wants €6 Billion From Cheap Parcels. Temu's Owner PDD Trades at 7x Earnings ©@small smiles from Getty Images via Canva, @dj_aof from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

PDD shares have fallen 39% over the past year to $83, leaving the stock at just 7.2x forward earnings.

Second-quarter revenue rose 8% to RMB112.4 billion, but net income fell 12% as PDD "stepped up" ecosystem investments.

Europe and the UK are tightening rules on cheap cross-border parcels and marketplace taxes, hitting Temu alongside Amazon.

PDD is expected to report third-quarter results around November 24, which should show whether profit has stopped falling.

PDD Holdings (PDD:NASDAQ) keeps getting cheaper while its cash pile keeps growing.

Shares closed at $83 on Friday, down 39% over the past year and far below their $139 52-week high. The company holds about $66 billion more cash than debt, roughly 56% of its market value.

Regulation explains much of the slide. Temu is in the crosshairs in Europe and the UK, and so is Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ): proposed EU fees on cheap parcels could raise €6 billion, and UK finance minister Healey plans to make online marketplaces collect tax from their sellers.

The other drag is self-inflicted. PDD is spending heavily on merchants, so profit is shrinking even as sales grow.

Sales up, profit down

The second quarter split growth from profit:

Revenue rose 8% to RMB112.4 billion ($16.6 billion), slightly below estimates.

Transaction services revenue grew 13% to RMB54.7 billion, while online marketing revenue rose about 3% to RMB57.6 billion.

Net income attributable to shareholders fell 12% to RMB27.2 billion, though adjusted earnings of RMB19.33 per ADS beat forecasts.

Operating profit rose 8% to RMB27.8 billion. Much of the net income damage came from a loss below the operating line.

"We stepped up our ecosystem investments in the second quarter," said Jun Liu, PDD's VP of Finance.

Top-line growth has cooled a lot since 2024…

PDD Holdings (PDD): total revenue, quarterly, RMB billions, Q2 2024–Q2 2026 (TIKR)

Growth slowed to 8% this quarter. That leaves transaction services doing most of the work, since online marketing barely grew.

Regulation is now a cost line

Cross-border pressure keeps building. In October, the EU accepted Temu's plan to remedy a Digital Services Act breach, and Temu agreed to data privacy restrictions to settle a Texas lawsuit.

Co-Chairman Lei Chen acknowledged the shift in the earnings release, saying "global trade and regulatory landscapes have continued to evolve, creating significant challenges while also presenting new opportunities."

The closest rival is feeling it too. Shein cut its Hong Kong IPO valuation to as much as $27 billion before a lackluster debut in September. PDD's $118 billion market cap dwarfs that, but investors are discounting both for the same rules.
